grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3774.summary: Second conclusion: theological discourse produces adherence (firm assent) in the mind of one who gives faith to Scripture, but not in others.
claims: Theological discourse produces adherence only in those who believe Scripture.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3779.summary: Third conclusion: the adherence acquired is not adherence with fear of the opposite (i.e., not opinion).
claims: Theological adherence is without formido.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3782.summary: Fourth conclusion: what is acquired is a kind of faith; hence the habit of theology so acquired is a creditive habit and an acquired faith.
claims: Theology acquired by theological discourse is an acquired faith.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3791.summary: First proof of the first conclusion: discourse that per se produces science proceeds from first, immediate, known propositions (Posterior Analytics I), but theological discourse proceeds from believed premises (article 2).
claims: Scientific discourse requires known immediate premises.
Theological discourse proceeds from believed premises.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3805.summary: Confirms: every discourse making one know is a demonstration, but theological discourse is not, else it would make a well-disposed unbeliever know and assent to theological conclusions.
claims: Theological discourse does not compel the assent of an unbeliever, so it is not demonstration.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3816.summary: Second proof: no discourse relying primarily on authority generates science, since authority generates only faith (Augustine: what we understand we owe to reason, what we believe to authority; De libero arbitrio); but all theological discourse so relies.
claims: Arguments from authority generate faith, not science.
Theological discourse relies primarily on authority.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3836.summary: Third proof: no theological discourse yields greater evidence or certainty about any theological truth than another theological discourse yields about a contingent truth not known by experience (e.g., that God will judge the world), since all proceed from scriptural authorities which as such give equal certainty; but no such contingent truth is known as scientific objects are; hence theological discourse does not per se produce science.
claims: All theological proofs yield equal evidence, grounded in scriptural authority.
Unexperienced contingent truths are not scientifically known.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3882.summary: Proof of the second conclusion: discourse that compels one believing Scripture to assent to something not formally in Scripture nor defined causes adherence, since one cannot naturally assent to premises without assenting to an evidently following conclusion; but a pagan who rejects Scripture gets no adherence even if he sees the consequence as clearly as a theologian.
claims: Assent to premises plus evident consequence compels assent to the conclusion.
Theological discourse generates no adherence in one who rejects Scripture.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3917.summary: Confirms the second conclusion by the authority of Pseudo-Dionysius' Divine Names cited in article 2.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3924.summary: Proof of the third conclusion: whoever adheres without fear to premises adheres without fear to a conclusion known to follow necessarily, since fear could arise neither from the firmly held premises nor from the known-necessary inference.
claims: Fearless adherence to premises transfers to necessarily following conclusions.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3938.summary: Confirms: it is naturally impossible to evidently cognize and indubitably assent that an antecedent cannot be true without its consequent, and indubitably assent to the antecedent, without indubitably assenting to the consequent; one firmly believing Scripture assents indubitably to the premises of a well-regulated theological discourse (the TEI reading 'dubitanter' appears to be a slip for 'indubitanter').
claims: Indubitable assent to antecedent and consequence entails indubitable assent to consequent.
The believer assents indubitably to scriptural premises.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3958.summary: Second proof: otherwise studying theology would be dangerous, since doubt about a conclusion known to follow from Scripture entails doubt about Scripture itself; and where there is doubt there is no faith (Hugh), and Augustine forbids saying 'perhaps' about matters of faith—so theological study would make one a heretic.
claims: Doubting a conclusion known to follow from Scripture entails doubting Scripture.
Doubt about matters of faith is incompatible with faith.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e3990.summary: Proof of the fourth conclusion: every assent without evidence and without fear is faith (from Hugh); the adherence caused in a firm believer is such; so the resulting habit is a creditive habit, an acquired habitual faith, and theology so taken is a kind of faith. Hence a pure pagan, giving faith to no part of Scripture, cannot be a theologian in this sense. But if theology is taken as the habit(s) by which one knows Scripture's sense, expounds and proves one text by another, and deduces further truths, it can be acquired by an unbeliever too. Then turns to the principal arguments.
claims: Assent without evidence and without fear is faith.
Theology as acquired adherence is an acquired faith.
A pure pagan cannot have theology in this sense.
Theology as exegetical and deductive skill can be acquired by an unbeliever.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e4036.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: denies that theological discourse yields a complex cognition superior to faith; nor is such discourse useless, for it yields the habit of proving theological truth from Scripture—thus defending faith against the impious and nourishing it in the faithful—and new explicit faith in truths not expressly in Scripture or defined, a very great fruit.
claims: Theological discourse does not yield cognition superior to faith.
It yields skill in proving and defending faith, and new explicit faith.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e4065.summary: Reply to the confirmation: concedes that the great theologian need not have greater cognition, or perhaps greater faith, than the simple believer regarding what the latter explicitly believes, but has another knowledge—of proving and defending—which is what Augustine speaks of.
claims: The theologian's advantage is skill in proving and defending, not superior cognition of the truths.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e4081.summary: Reply to the second argument (Augustine's hope to reach certain knowledge through faith): first reading—'certain knowledge' means the clear vision succeeding faith in heaven, supported by De Trinitate 9 that certain cognition is perfected only after this life, face to face.
claims: Augustine's 'certain knowledge' may mean the beatific vision.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e4101.summary: Second reading: Augustine hoped even in this life to reach certain knowledge by special divine revelation and infusion, as God has often done for true believers; De libero arbitrio II supports this (we find what we seek with God demonstrating and illuminating within). But such knowledge is not the theology commonly acquired by theological discourse.
claims: God may infuse certain knowledge of credibilia in this life.
Such infused knowledge is not acquired theology.

grvnZZ-d1e97-d1e4143.summary: Reply to the third argument: in De Trinitate 14 Augustine calls scientia the habit(s) by which one can defend faith; this is a knowing of a sort, but not knowing that things are as the conclusion signifies, which was the question.
claims: Augustine's scientia is the know-how of defending faith, not demonstrative knowledge of conclusions.

grvnZZ-d1e97.summary: Question 1 of the prologue asks whether properly scientific knowledge (scientia) of the theological object is acquired through theological discourse. Gregory works through four articles. Article 1 asks what the object of demonstrative science is. Against the view that the object is the conclusion, and against the view that it is the extramental thing, Gregory argues that it is the total significate of the conclusion (significatum totale, the complexe significabile). This significate is 'something' in the broad senses of res/aliquid but is not an existing entity. It is true and necessary in a de dicto sense, and on the preferred account it is true by denomination from uncreated truth. Article 2 asks what makes discourse theological. Gregory rejects the view that theological discourse argues from probable premises to articles already determined by the Church. He holds instead that theological principles are the truths of Scripture and theological conclusions are whatever follows necessarily from Scripture, whether or not the Church has defined it. Ecclesial authority is a motive of faith, not a theological premise. Article 3 asks which intellectual act is scientia. Gregory identifies the demonstrative mental conclusion with both the assent and the cognition: enunciating, cognizing, and assenting are one act. He grounds this in a typology of mental propositions (language-images; natural cognitive enunciations; natural non-cognitive assents such as belief and opinion) and denies that mental propositions are composed of subject- and predicate-cognitions. Article 4 rejects the view that theology is science subalternated to the science of God and the blessed: knowledge must be caused by the knower's own cognition of principles. Gregory concludes that theological discourse does not per se produce science. In those who believe Scripture it produces firm, fearless adherence, which is an acquired faith. Theology in this sense is a creditive habit. Theology as exegetical and deductive skill, by contrast, can belong even to an unbeliever. The usefulness of theology lies in proving, defending, and extending faith, not in cognition superior to faith.
claims: The object of demonstrative science is the total significate of the conclusion, neither the proposition nor the extramental thing.
Propositional significates are not existing entities, yet they are true and necessary objects of science.
Theological discourse proceeds from Scripture or from what follows necessarily from it, not from merely probable premises.
Theological conclusions include every truth that follows necessarily from Scripture, whether or not the Church has determined it.
In demonstrative knowledge, the mental conclusion, the cognition, and the assent are one and the same act.
Mental propositions are not composed of distinct subject and predicate cognitions.
Theology is not a science subalternated to divine science, since science requires the knower's own evidence of principles.
Theological discourse yields in believers an acquired faith without fear of the opposite, not scientia.
Theology's value lies in proving, defending, and extending faith from Scripture.
